Podcast Source: The Super Cycle; Compiled by: Deep Tide TechFlow

Accompanied by the federal prison's automated voice prompt "Call from federal detention center," former FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried (SBF) received an 82-minute high-energy, in-depth interview with 14-year-old tech blogger Eli Goldfine at the Metropolitan Detention Center (MDC Brooklyn). In what is considered one of the most information-dense conversations in recent years, the imprisoned SBF unusually broke his silence, comprehensively recounting his cognitive landscape, investment journey, and extreme philosophy.

From the behind-the-scenes maneuvering that led FTX Ventures to inject $500 million into Anthropic, to the radical projections of the future AI landscape reaching hundreds of billions or even trillions of dollars; from the cold scrutiny of traditional software moats and Coinbase's brand value, to confronting the philosophical questions of Tyler Cowen's "51/49 coin toss: destroy the world or multiply the benefits" and the gamble of personal freedom; and finally, to the final confession that "the outcome brought by FTX was not worth it, and all the truth was distorted by the winner's filter when the crisis broke out," SBF presents the complete mental world of a genius operator after falling from grace with the most naked thought process. Guest: Sam Bankman-Fried (Founder and former CEO of FTX, currently serving time in federal prison; a core practitioner of effective altruism) Host: Eli Goldfine (Head of the 14-year-old tech and prediction podcast The Super Cycle, Twitter @realTomBayes) Original Title: EXCLUSIVE: I'm 14, and I just interviewed Sam Bankman-Fried Air Date: November 20, 2026 (Beijing Time: 2026-11-21) Key Takeaways Summary: The greatest torment in prison is the isolation from cutting-edge information: SBF He frankly admitted that thinking about the case while in prison provided no new insights to the outside world. What truly tormented him was the inability to keep up with the real-world performance of large language models, code details, market trends, and due diligence on startups. This lack of cutting-edge micro-input made effective thinking extremely difficult. The story behind Anthropic's early $500 million investment: FTX Ventures practically monopolized Anthropic's entire Series B funding round. The reason for not injecting more computing power was that excessive cash could easily lead to corporate extravagance (such as blindly buying users), and the team was unwilling to excessively dilute equity; blind expansion would be counterproductive. The AI ​​industry will reach a trillion-dollar dominance: In the next decade, AI will inevitably become a pillar or even a dominant sector of the global economy; since only a few top laboratories can compete for the throne (Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepMind, xAI), it is entirely logical from an economic perspective that leading institutions enjoy trillion-dollar valuations. Traditional software companies haven't been completely condemned by AI: Physical industries (such as steel and mining) are lagging behind in the impact of AI; for pure software and financial institutions, even if competitors use AI to replicate the same functions at extremely low cost, they cannot easily overthrow the pioneers, because the real moat of companies like Coinbase and Robinhood is their unbreakable brand trust. The p(doom) assessment falls into a complex gray area of ​​around 25%: SBF believes the probability of humanity being destroyed or facing a survival catastrophe due to AI is between 10% and 50% (median about 25%); the form of the catastrophe is not simply uncontrolled nuclear weapons, but more likely complex gray scenarios, such as the complete marginalization and elimination of those who did not upload their human consciousness. The political prediction market was an unfulfilled ambition of FTX: In essence, prediction markets are futures contracts with specific settlement rules. FTX initially conducted hundreds of millions of dollars worth of US election predictions in offshore markets, but was limited by its inability to obtain a license from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC). The explosive growth of Kalshi and Polymarket validated the potential of this sector. There is strong skepticism about the information throughput efficiency of print books: SBF reiterated its famous view that most books should be condensed into six-paragraph blog posts; in contrast, streaming media (such as Netflix) have a much higher information throughput and expressive depth per unit of time than books burdened by excessive preamble. Extreme Expectations and the Real-World Disillusionment of the 51/49 Coin Flip: Under theoretically purely linear expected value, the 51% chance of doubling and the 49% chance of world destruction is mathematically valid; however, in the real world, destruction carries the irreversible cost of extinction, and its real utility diminishes marginally. Faced with the possibility of betting 51/49 on immediate release from prison, the individual risk utility function dictates that the theoretical gamble cannot be simply applied to reality. A Sobering Reflection on the FTX Outcome: When asked "Was it all worth it?", SBF clearly stated, "I can't honestly say it was worth it; if it hadn't been a disaster, it should have been." In times of crisis, people easily lose their rationality and core judgment, and subsequently, history is reshaped and distorted through the lens of the victors. The survival guidelines for the new generation of 14-year-olds: Stop obsessing over high-frequency trading on Wall Street to "earn to give"; the priority is to fully understand AI, get involved in AI security, or find practical ways to automate infrastructure with AI.

Key Insights

On the brutal barrier of information asymmetry in prison: "If you want to create value at the forefront, you need to master hundreds or thousands of tiny details: on which tasks does the large model excel, where does it still falter, what is being discussed at the forefront of the industry, and what changes have occurred in the microstructure of the market. Within the high walls of a federal prison, obtaining these details is almost an impossible task."

On Anthropic's valuation and competitive advantage: "If you believe that AI will become a core sector dominating trillions of dollars globally over the next decade, and that only a handful of top-tier core labs can sit at this table, then it's entirely reasonable for each leading company to receive trillions of dollars in market capitalization. Anthropic's strength in code generation and software engineering tools remains among the world's best."

On the real barriers of brand and technology: "Many programmers think technology is everything, but look at Coinbase or..." Why are companies like Robinhood worth tens of billions of dollars? It's definitely not because they possess proprietary algorithms that can't be replicated, but because they have the brand trust that comes from the mouths of retail consumers across the US. Even if competitors could replicate the exact same software with AI at almost zero cost, they simply couldn't buy this brand asset. Regarding a radical critique of print books: "I still believe that if you write a book, it often means you've made a mistake; it should have been a six-paragraph blog post. Books have too low an information throughput, filled with lengthy, useless narratives; in the same unit of time, high-density visual and audiovisual input can convey far more effective information." Regarding a realistic reflection on the 51/49 coin toss: "In pure ivory tower expected value theory, you can extrapolate doubling global utility to gamble on 49%..." The probability of destruction; but in the real world there is an irreversible risk of systemic zeroing out, and any positive utility has its limit of diminishing marginal utility. Once you include the fatal cost of destruction in the model, you simply wouldn't dare to toss most coins in reality. "

Regarding the final conclusion of the rise and fall of FTX: "I want to comfort myself with the illusion that it was all worth it, but I can't say that against my conscience. It should have been worth it if I hadn't completely messed everything up at the last minute. At the moment of the outbreak of an extreme crisis, panic distorts all advice and decisions, and after the smoke clears, all historical narratives are inevitably completely reconstructed by the victor's position."

Prison Life and Cognitive Barriers: The Black Box World Without Microscopic Details

Eli Goldfine: Welcome to The Super Cycle, I'm Eli Goldfine.

Prison Life and Cognitive Barriers: The Black Box World Without Microscopic Details

Eli Goldfine: Welcome to The Super Cycle, I'm Eli Goldfine.

Today we are honored to connect with Sam Bankman-Fried (SBF). My team and I have been coordinating and preparing for this for months, and it's the most information-dense in-depth interview since the podcast's inception. Hello, Sam, can you hear me? Sam Bankman-Fried: Yes, I can hear you perfectly well. Eli Goldfine: It's a pleasure to connect with you. I've seen many of your recent interviews, and most of the outside attention has been focused on the collapse of FTX and your daily life in prison. In prison, you have ample time for solitude and reflection. What issues do you spend most of your time thinking about? Sam Bankman-Fried: That's a natural question. Obviously, I do spend a significant amount of time reviewing my own case, reflecting on what happened, and thinking about what I can still do about it. But I'm well aware that these reflections don't offer much added value to people in the outside world. I try to focus my energy on what I can still do in the future. But in the prison environment, productive forward-thinking is extremely difficult. Eli Goldfine: Why is forward-thinking so difficult in prison? Is it because of a lack of key information? Sam Bankman-Fried: It's not a lack of any single piece of information, but a lack of countless small but crucial inputs. If you want to be at the forefront of human cognition and business to predict the future, you must master a vast amount of dynamic details: How exactly do cutting-edge large language models evolve? In which specific tasks have their evaluation curves broken through human limits, and in which areas are they still inadequate? You must test these technologies firsthand in practice and talk to the people who build these models on the front lines every day. The same applies from a financial perspective. You have to keep a close eye on the market every day, observe fund flows and transaction structures, build a network of contacts, communicate with emerging startups, discuss their business models, and conduct in-depth due diligence. These are all things I would do every day if I were outside, but behind the high walls of a federal detention center, obtaining any information becomes extremely difficult, even nearly impossible. Eli Goldfine: If you could obtain information in prison, which dimensions of information do you think would be most valuable for your deductions about the real world? Sam Bankman-Fried: Again, it's not a single breaking news story, but thousands of micro-variables. For example, the architectural evolution of cutting-edge models, the actual implementation threshold of code generation, the cash flow trajectory of startups in real business environments, and the actual purchasing intentions of customers in different industries. Without these micro-details, a macro framework derived purely in isolation is often extremely fragile. Eli Goldfine: You obviously can't spend all your time thinking about the case. Besides the case, what broader issues do you also think about? Sam Bankman-Fried: Yes, but a lot of thinking is still highly constrained by my current physical environment, because this is the only world where I can get direct, firsthand feedback. It's not that it's that important, but I do spend a lot of time thinking about the criminal justice system. Not just about my personal experience, but the absurd logic that the entire justice system exhibits on a general level. Reflections on the Federal Criminal Justice System: Fabricated Charges, Performance Indicators, and Reverse Incentives Eli Goldfine: In the context of your personal case, what specific general judicial problems have you observed? Sam Bankman-Fried: As the saying goes, if you have a hammer, everything looks like a nail. The justice system has the exact same pattern. If you establish a federal task force specifically to combat a particular type of crime, that task force will frantically search for leads, regardless of whether the crime actually exists. Once the task force's size and budget exceed the actual scale of that type of crime in society, it will inevitably begin fabricating cases to arrest people for behaviors that don't constitute crimes at all. This distortion has been widely exposed in the federal anti-drug system over the past few decades, and in the last decade, this trend has permeated and spread to every area of ​​federal justice. Eli Goldfine: For example, in which specific areas? Sam Bankman-Fried: For example, the massive federal cybercrime investigation agency, originally established to combat extreme aggression, is now extending its reach to private text message conversations and normal interactions between lovers. Countless completely innocent people are prosecuted and arrested simply because prosecutors need these cases as performance indicators for their promotions and raises. The case of former Honduran President Juan Orlando Hernandez is a prime example of how outrageous the consequences can be when the prosecution system completely spirals out of control. Eli Goldfine: Do you still believe that white-collar crime should be punished with imprisonment? Sam Bankman-Fried: Absolutely not. Putting white-collar criminals in jail does nothing to help society. The only thing it does is rip decades out of someone's life and impose a huge financial burden on taxpayers to run the prisons. If you're purely motivated by revenge, then it achieves its purpose; but I don't believe this system can reform anyone. Eli Goldfine: What do you think is the most reasonable course of action for those who actually commit financial fraud? Sam Bankman-Fried: It depends on the specific details of the case. But in the vast majority of commercial and financial cases, civil proceedings are a far more sophisticated and rational path than criminal trials. Civil remedies can address issues through massive fines, amendments to business contracts, restrictions on professional qualifications, and asset seizure. More importantly, as a modern society, we must learn to reduce our blind overconfidence. We often assume we can accurately see the truth and that those punished are necessarily bad people, but in reality, many who end up on trial are simply scapegoats used by certain forces to divert attention from their own problems. Eli Goldfine: Is improving the judicial system a priority for effective altruistic communities? Sam Bankman-Fried: From a utility expectation perspective, this area is extremely complex. The social value of judicial reform is undoubtedly enormous, but it faces extremely strong political resistance and institutional inertia. When an interest group forms a massive industrial loop through the incarceration of people, it is extremely difficult for external forces to drive fundamental change. Eli Goldfine: In your opinion, what is the easiest low-hanging fruit to pluck in improving the criminal justice system? Sam Bankman-Fried: The easiest to promote and one that can immediately unleash huge economic benefits is a complete overhaul of pre-trial detention and sentencing standards for nonviolent crimes. The current system is rife with impoverished people detained for extended periods because they cannot afford meager bail, and working-class people sentenced to decades in prison for drug offenses. Providing them with formal market-based job training and community corrections, rather than directly imprisoning them and severing their social connections, is the most cost-effective reform approach. AI Industry Endgame Prospects: Trillion-Dollar Valuations and a Few Oligopolistic Table Eli Goldfine: Let's talk about cutting-edge technology. Anthropic is about to launch its IPO, and external expectations for its valuation are pushing towards hundreds of billions or even trillions of dollars. As an early lead investor in Anthropic's $500 million Series B round, what's your view on the current valuations of these large model labs? Sam Bankman-Fried: I think they are absolutely worth that price, and even more in the future. From a macro-business perspective: Throughout human economic history, the total market capitalization of all the core pillars that truly support the operation of human civilization has ranged from trillions to tens of trillions of dollars. In the next five to ten years, AI is highly likely to grow into the most core, and even the most dominant, economic industry globally. Eli Goldfine: If the entire AI sector reaches a market capitalization of tens of trillions of dollars in the future, how will this value be distributed by the market? Sam Bankman-Fried: Assuming that two-thirds of the future multi-trillion dollar market capitalization is reserved for innovative applications and emerging companies that have not yet been born, then the remaining segment will still have at least ten trillion dollars shared by existing leading underlying model companies. However, if you count carefully, how many top-tier labs globally are truly qualified to sit at this core table? OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, plus xAI—you can count them on one hand. When a multi-trillion dollar sector is ultimately divided among a handful of top oligopolies, the inevitable result is that the intrinsic value of each top leader must be measured in trillions of dollars. Anthropic is undoubtedly among the top two globally. Eli Goldfine: Why do you rate Anthropic so highly? Is it because of the performance of the Claude series models in benchmark tests? Sam Bankman-Fried: Benchmark scores are important, and the outside world can see Claude's strong reputation in everyday conversations and mass-market consumer applications. But Anthropic's true core asset that sets it apart is its absolute dominance in software engineering and professional development tools. Their development kits and code understanding capabilities for engineers are among the best in the world, serving as the core working machine for the future digital society's transition to AI automation. Eli Goldfine: If the next decade sees a complete super-intelligent arms race, what do you think the world will look like? Sam Bankman-Fried: The distribution of productivity across society will be completely reshaped. In the past few years, while large models have evolved exponentially, social order has remained seemingly calm because their absolute capabilities are still below the human average. However, once a certain critical point is crossed, in fields such as programming, law, financial modeling, and drug development, machines will produce hundreds of times more than humans. The speed of wealth creation will accelerate dramatically, but how to distribute the dividends brought by this computing power will become the focus of the most intense geopolitical game globally. Eli Goldfine: Many people have been curious about FTX Ventures' almost complete Series B funding round for Anthropic. Since you were so confident about the future of AI at the time, why didn't you offer a larger check, such as injecting $1 billion or even $2 billion to allow them unlimited purchases of graphics processing units (GPUs) and the construction of data centers? Sam Bankman-Fried: There are two key considerations here. First, from the perspective of the founding team, any excellent team does not want to excessively dilute their control and equity stake in the company in the early stages; they are only willing to raise the amount of funds necessary for the current stage of development. Secondly, while many companies in business history have died due to a lack of funds, it's equally common for companies to be bloated by excessive cash flow and ultimately devoured by their own capital. Many startups, after raising astronomical sums of money, often experience a blind anxiety of "I must spend this money," squandering huge sums on meaningless marketing or reckless expansion, ultimately losing their respect for tackling core technologies. In the early stages of building large models, iterating the model architecture and validating algorithms requires a steady R&D cycle; it's not something that can be achieved simply by piling on computing power. Anthropic's planning for the use of funds was very rational at the time, and our investment perfectly met their core need to start training the next generation of large models. Eli Goldfine: How did FTX Ventures operate at that time? What role did you personally play in the specific investment decisions? Sam Bankman-Fried: Many early deals were discovered by our team members in their daily work, including a large number of early crypto-native investments, many of which achieved several times the asset value annually. Anthropic and Solana are similar; they were disruptive projects we initially came into deep contact with by chance. As we grew, we brought in professional partners to build a formal investment structure. For ordinary deals, I tend to fully trust the analytical team responsible for due diligence; but for strategically significant bets like Anthropic, I follow up deeply on a weekly or even more frequent basis, exploring how we can assist them in terms of underlying computing power, finance, and resource networks. Eli Goldfine: When you first contacted the Dario Amodei team, what impressed you most about them? Sam Bankman-Fried: Extreme rigor and focus. When Dario and his team spun out of OpenAI, their goal was very clear: to create cutting-edge security models with high interpretability and alignment guarantees. They didn't engage in flashy marketing demonstrations to grab short-term attention; every capital expenditure was extremely restrained, focused on key computing clusters and engineering talent recruitment. This kind of engineering culture is extremely rare in today's fast-paced Silicon Valley.

The Existence Crisis and Brand Moat of Traditional Software Companies: Why AI Can't Kill Coinbase?

Eli Goldfine: With the explosive growth of cutting-edge model capabilities, many traditional software companies are facing enormous existential anxiety. Do you think those traditional software companies that haven't deeply integrated AI are doomed?

Sam Bankman-Fried: It's not that absolute. First, many industries in the real economy have a natural physical buffer against AI penetration, such as steel smelting and underground mining. No matter how smart AI is, it can't mine ore overnight.

Secondly, for purely digital software, the deciding factor is not just the efficiency of the underlying code. Many people severely underestimate the absolute moat of "brand." Suppose a competitor uses the latest large-scale modeling tools to clone a software product with almost identical functionality at extremely low cost. Does this mean users will abandon the original product? Absolutely not. Eli Goldfine: Like Coinbase or Robinhood? Sam Bankman-Fried: Absolutely. Why do Coinbase and Robinhood enjoy market capitalizations of hundreds of billions of dollars? Is it because they possess top-secret matching engine code that other teams absolutely cannot replicate? Of course not. Their most valuable asset is brand recognition—the trust endorsement that millions of ordinary retail investors across the United States spontaneously give when they want to buy or sell digital assets. Even if a new team could rewrite a front-end and transaction system using AI at almost zero cost, it simply couldn't buy back the brand reputation built up over many years in a short period. A strong brand often allows traditional companies to maintain long-term resilience in the face of homogenized underlying products. Eli Goldfine: So what kind of traditional software companies will be eliminated the fastest? Sam Bankman-Fried: Middleware software that relies purely on feature stacking, lacking both brand awareness and deep data network effects. If your product is just a simple ticket management or form filling tool, with no emotional or brand connection between users and you, then AI-native tools will completely crush it in a very short time at one-tenth the cost.

The Real Alpha in Tech Investment: Minimalist AI Native Teams vs. Garbage Companies Riding the Hype

Eli Goldfine: So where do you think the real excess returns (Alpha) in the current tech investment field are hidden?

Sam Bankman-Fried: The real Alpha lies in the ability to see through the bubble. Currently, half of the startups on the market are blatantly using the AI ​​label on their business plans, even a company selling T-shirts claims to use AI to design patterns. These are essentially all industrial garbage.

At the same time, the truly huge opportunities lie in a very small number of native teams with only two or three core members: they completely rely on the AI ​​toolchain to reconstruct the traditional enterprise workflow that requires hundreds or thousands of people to maintain with incredible streamlined efficiency, and quickly grow into super species with valuations of tens of millions to hundreds of millions of dollars.

Distinguishing between genuine breakthroughs and speculative hype is the most crucial watershed moment in investing today. Eli Goldfine: If you were freely managing your own funds today, would you return to this type of investment? Sam Bankman-Fried: Absolutely. If I were outside, I would actively seek out and heavily invest in these two- or three-person super-species. They don't have the bureaucratic infighting of traditional companies; each member can leverage a large model to access the output equivalent to a complete engineering department. The explosive power and profit margins resulting from this streamlined efficiency are completely unimaginable in traditional organizational structures. Biopharmaceuticals and Longevity Technology: Regulatory Constraints and Accelerated AI R&D Eli Goldfine: Let's talk about biotechnology. FTX funded many anti-aging, longevity, and gene therapy projects in its early days. What are your thoughts on the progress in the biopharmaceutical field? Sam Bankman-Fried: Biotechnology is a field with enormous potential, but its biggest bottleneck is not the intelligence of scientists, but the outdated regulatory system. The clinical approval process of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is extremely lengthy and costly; a new drug often requires billions of dollars and up to a decade to reach the market. Many early-stage therapies that could potentially save lives are effectively stalled in the lab because they cannot raise the astronomical sums needed to complete Phase III clinical trials. We aimed to provide early-stage catalytic funding for these high-risk, high-reward cutting-edge endeavors. Eli Goldfine: Will AI change this? Sam Bankman-Fried: AI has already demonstrated disruptive power in protein structure prediction, molecular docking, and compound screening. AI can compress early-stage lab screenings that previously took years or even decades into just a few months. But ultimately, all drugs still must undergo physical human clinical trials. Without fundamental reform of outdated and rigid regulatory processes, mere technological acceleration will still be significantly slowed down by offline administrative barriers. Eli Goldfine: How do you think the clinical approval process should be optimized for rare or fatal diseases? Sam Bankman-Fried: More flexible informed consent and parallel pathways should be introduced. For patients with terminal illnesses for whom modern medicine has run out of options, if they are fully informed and willing to try innovative therapies in Phase I or II clinical trials, regulatory agencies should not rudely deprive them of their right to life. Dynamic tracking through real-world data (RWD) is far more ethically conscious than mechanically waiting ten years for a Phase III double-blind trial. Politics, Regulation, and Reflections on the Biden Administration: Encryption Hostility and the Democratic Party's Loss Eli Goldfine: Let's talk about politics and macro-regulation. Over the past four years, the Biden administration has taken a very aggressive stance on technology and financial regulation, particularly the Securities and Exchange Commission's (SEC) comprehensive enforcement action against the cryptocurrency industry. How would you rate the Biden administration's regulatory performance? Sam Bankman-Fried: I think the Biden administration's performance in this area has been extremely disappointing. Not only against the crypto industry, but across the entire technology innovation sector, regulators have shown a deep-seated bureaucratic hostility. Instead of committing to establishing a clear, enforceable, and innovation-promoting legal framework, they have relentlessly targeted compliant domestic companies with raids, directly leading to a massive outflow of top tech talent and innovative capital to offshore markets. Eli Goldfine: You made substantial donations during your political campaigns. Why do you think there's a disconnect between the political establishment's understanding of the tech industry and reality? Sam Bankman-Fried: Many politicians and regulators simply don't understand the underlying logic of technology; they're only concerned with political narratives and power struggles. In many policy-making processes, the decision-making basis is not which option is most beneficial to the socio-economic situation, but which option can bring the most votes and political capital. I believe the Democratic Party has seriously lost its way on many economic and technological issues over the past decade. Eli Goldfine: Should technology companies slow down to ensure security in the face of international technological competition? Sam Bankman-Fried: This is an extremely dangerous game theory trap. If a company with a security-oriented philosophy unilaterally slows down, while other global competitors, even unfriendly countries, are racing ahead, then unilateral self-restraint will not make the world safer; instead, it will directly hand over control of cutting-edge technologies to competitors who completely disregard security and ethics. The ideal situation is for all major stakeholders to reach a substantial security agreement, but in real-world geopolitics, this is extremely difficult. The Essence and Explosion of Political Prediction Markets: From FTX 2020 Election Contracts to Kalshi and Polymarket Eli Goldfine: Let's talk about financial innovation. Kalshi's valuation has recently skyrocketed, and Polymarket has seen astonishing trading volume in global political elections. I heard that one of your original ideas at the inception of FTX was to create a global political prediction market? Sam Bankman-Fried: From the underlying logic of financial engineering, a prediction market is essentially a futures contract that is settled in cash based on the outcome of a specific real-world event. They are not fundamentally different from Bitcoin or crude oil futures. During the 2020 US presidential election, FTX International ran the most active Trump vs. Biden prediction contracts on the entire network, with trading volumes reaching hundreds of millions of dollars. From day one, we aspired to expand this market, but the biggest obstacle has always been regulatory licensing. Because of the lack of domestic license from the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), we strictly prohibited U.S. users from participating at the time, and centralized exchanges mandated comprehensive Know Your Customer (KYC) verification. Eli Goldfine: Why did Kalshi and Polymarket explode in this cycle? Sam Bankman-Fried: They followed two different paths. Kalshi spent years obtaining a compliant license domestically through legal proceedings and formal procedures; while Polymarket, relying on offshore and decentralized architecture, amassed enormous liquidity globally. This fully proves our judgment at the time: the human need to price major historical events is universal and real. Besides prediction markets, tokenized equities still have enormous growth potential. The underlying settlement system of traditional stock trading markets is extremely outdated and inefficient. A 24/7 seamless clearing system based on blockchain has a completely superior advantage in terms of infrastructure experience.

AGI Critical Point and p(doom) Assessment: The Gray Dilemma of 25% Extinction Probability and Consciousness Upload

Eli Goldfine: Many people are discussing when Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) and even Superintelligence (ASI) will arrive. What is your personal expectation for the timeline of AGI?

Sam Bankman-Fried: I don't think the arrival of AGI will be a clear-cut, black-and-white, single-point discrete event. It is more likely to be a gradual process of continuous evolution and replacement.

For a long time, although AI's computing power has been doubling, its intelligence level is far below the human baseline, so it has had almost no substantial impact on the real world. But when its intelligence gradually approaches that of humans and breaks the critical point in specific vertical fields, qualitative changes will spread at an extremely rapid speed. We have already seen this trend in software development, advanced mathematical derivations, and game theory strategies.

In the next three to five years, key sectors of human society will be deeply taken over by AI, one after another. Eli Goldfine: In the effective altruism community, AI safety and the probability of human extinction have always been the core debate topics. You have never publicly given your personal p(doom) (the probability of AI causing human extinction or complete destruction) specific value. Could you give a precise judgment today? Sam Bankman-Fried: If I had to give a value, I think it's below 50% but above 10%, roughly in the 25% range. But one point must be clarified: In my assessment model, catastrophic scenarios are often not like those in Hollywood movies where a clearly hostile, out-of-control AI suddenly gains control of the nuclear button and declares war on all of humanity. In reality, what is more likely to occur is an extremely complex gray ethical dilemma. Eli Goldfine: For example, what kind of gray dilemma? Sam Bankman-Fried: For example, mind uploading. If future technology advances to the point where humans can digitize and upload their entire brain consciousness to the cloud, those intelligent beings who achieve digital immortality will surpass physical humans exponentially in computing power and evolutionary speed. In that scenario, will the original humans remaining in the physical world be completely eliminated and marginalized? Is this process, which leads to the de facto extinction of the physical Homo sapiens species, a catastrophe for human civilization? Different people will give diametrically opposed philosophical answers. Once you take these evolutionary paths, fraught with ethical ambiguity, into consideration, the probability assessment of survival risk will fluctuate wildly between 20% and 60%. AI Agents and Future Workflows: Super Research Assistants Ten Times More Powerful Than Humans

Eli Goldfine: If a super intelligent assistant emerged in the future that surpasses you in logical reasoning and decision-making expectations, would you be willing to entrust it with all your personal decision-making power?

Sam Bankman-Fried: It depends on its optimization objective function. Is it to maximize its own survival probability, or to maximize the well-being of all sentient beings, or to faithfully fulfill the objectives I entrusted to it?

If its core alignment objective is to act as a loyal, meticulous, and rationally prudent research assistant, capable of completing intensive due diligence and deductions that would normally take a whole day in a minute at a speed a hundred times faster than humans, then I would absolutely be willing to entrust it with a large number of specific execution and analysis tasks. But the ultimate value orientation and ethical bottom line must always be anchored to the core needs of humanity itself.

Eli Goldfine: How will this kind of super assistant disrupt the finance and investment industry? Sam Bankman-Fried: The pyramid structure of traditional investment institutions, composed of hundreds or thousands of junior analysts, will collapse instantly. A partner, working with several autonomous AI agents specifically designed for cross-checking financial statements, cleaning macroeconomic data, and tracking public opinion, can accomplish the output of an entire investment bank building. The competition between institutions will no longer depend on how many top university graduates they hire, but on who has a deeper understanding of the optimization strategies and underlying logic of AI agents. Why such extreme skepticism towards printed books? The information throughput and the devastating impact of audiovisual media. Eli Goldfine: Let's discuss a very interesting topic in life. Many intelligent people pride themselves on being well-read, but I remember you once made a very famous counterintuitive statement: "I have serious doubts about the value of books; most books should be written as a six-paragraph blog post." Now that you're in prison, how many books have you read? Has your opinion changed? Sam Bankman-Fried: In prison, I didn't have many choices, so I read a lot, but this only strengthened my belief that my initial judgment was correct. If you write an entire book, it often means you haven't even figured out your core argument. In a book of hundreds of pages, the truly valuable core insights can often be fully explained in a few paragraphs; the remaining ninety percent is just piling up lengthy examples, foreshadowing, and irrelevant narratives to make up the book's thickness. Eli Goldfine: What types of books have you mainly read in prison? Is there any that you think is worth reading? Sam Bankman-Fried: I've read a lot of science fiction. But to be honest, most science fiction is just so-so. If I had the option, I'd rather watch hard science fiction series on Netflix. A very few exceptionally well-written science fiction works might barely reach the level of a mediocre TV series, but they still can't compete with streaming media in terms of information transmission. Eli Goldfine: Compared to books, which medium do you value more for its information transmission efficiency? Sam Bankman-Fried: High-density audiovisual media far surpasses printed text in terms of information throughput per unit of time. In a good movie or in-depth TV series, visual images, characters' micro-expressions, sound effects, editing rhythm, and dialogue simultaneously transmit dozens of dimensions of information to your brain within a single second. This high-density emotional and cognitive resonance is something that the extremely inefficient one-way printed text simply cannot match.

The Boundary Between Effective Altruism (EA) and Quantitative Metrics: QALYs and Distortion of Real-World Assessments

Eli Goldfine: In the effective altruism community, people are accustomed to using rigorous mathematical formulas and qualitatively adjusted life years (QALYs) to quantify the expected utility of every charitable expenditure. After being imprisoned, how do you view this purely quantitative philosophy of philanthropy?

Sam Bankman-Fried: Purely theoretical expected values ​​are elegant in the world of pure mathematics, but the complexity of the real world lies in the fact that the quantifiable metrics you choose are often not the core values ​​of humanity's ultimate concerns.

When you simplify complex real-world problems into a single-dimensional number in pursuit of mathematical measurability, you easily fall into the trap of the blind men and the elephant.

For example, funding mosquito nets to prevent malaria is extremely easy to quantify in terms of cost and short-term benefits; however, funding institutional development, breakthroughs in basic science, or the prevention of civilizational catastrophes has long-term impacts that are full of unquantifiable parameters in mathematical models. To abandon those far-reaching attempts that truly determine the fate of civilization simply because they cannot be precisely quantified is itself the greatest betrayal of rationality. Eli Goldfine: Does this mean that excessive quantification has become a dogmatic trap of effective altruism? Sam Bankman-Fried: Indeed. When people are overly obsessed with the verifiability of mathematical models, they instinctively reject truly disruptive but uncertain grand propositions. A healthy evaluation framework must acknowledge the boundaries of human cognition and maintain a dynamic balance between quantitative precision and intuitive perspective.

51/49 The Extreme Philosophical Question of a Coin Toss: Pure Expectation Value vs. Irreversible Destruction and Diminishing Margins

Eli Goldfine: I'd like to discuss a well-known thought experiment with you. Economist Tyler Cowen once posed a hypothetical question to you: If there's a coin, heads has a 51% probability of doubling the overall utility of the Earth, and tails has a 49% probability of causing the complete destruction of the Earth, would you choose to toss the coin? At the time, your answer was yes. Today, in prison, do you still adhere to this pure expectation value logic?

Sam Bankman-Fried: This is a classic debate topic that is extremely fascinating in philosophy and probability theory.

If you strictly limit the problem to purely mathematical assumptions and a linear expected utility function, the mathematical answer is obvious: 51% multiplied by 2 is greater than 1, the expected value is positive, and any staunch expectancy maximizer must logically accept this gamble. However, in the real world, this thought experiment is instinctively rejected by most normal people because it ignores fundamental constraints in the real world that cannot be simply abstracted. Eli Goldfine: What exactly are these ignored real-world constraints? Sam Bankman-Fried: First, destruction is absolutely irreversible (Catastrophic Ruin). In a game of probability, if you have a certain probability of going to zero and permanently exiting the game, you will never have the chance to enjoy the benefits of subsequent positive expected values. Second, utility is never strictly linear; it suffers from strong diminishing marginal utility. In reality, the increased happiness brought to human civilization by doubling Earth's utility is far from offsetting the infinite suffering caused by a 49% probability of complete annihilation. Applying an extreme model stripped of diminishing marginal utility and bankruptcy protection directly to the real world often leads to extremely dangerous judgment biases. Eli Goldfine: If delaying technological development could result in a lower probability of destruction, would you support slowing down? Sam Bankman-Fried: If, in a theoretical model, delaying humanity's entry into superintelligence by a hundred years could reduce the probability of civilization's destruction by even just 1%, then from the macroscopic long-term perspective of the universe's future billions of years, this hundred-year stagnation is mathematically worthwhile. Because the future of the universe is infinitely long, and once civilization reaches zero, it is completely finished. High-expectation-value games in reality: If you were to gamble 51/49 on personal freedom, would you give it up? Eli Goldfine: What if this gamble were replaced with real-world stakes that directly affect you? Suppose you have a coin toss where there's a 51% chance you'll be released from prison immediately tomorrow without charge, and a 49% chance your sentence will double or you'll even be sentenced to death. Would you flip the coin? Sam Bankman-Fried: This vividly illustrates why utility functions in reality aren't linear. When it comes to core assets like personal freedom and life, people's aversion to extreme downside risks is immense. If I were released tomorrow, my life would undoubtedly improve dramatically; but if the cost is a nearly 50% chance of enduring a longer or even fatal abyss, that risk premium is unacceptable. This is why complex decisions in reality should never be made hastily based on a rough expected value. Eli Goldfine: Many people believe that your past investment and business decisions were products of this philosophy of extreme expectations. Do you agree with this assessment? Sam Bankman-Fried: I think the outside world has oversimplified my thinking. In regular trading, we pay extreme attention to hedging and risk exposure management; however, in the event of an extreme crisis, the safety cushion of many theoretical models can be instantly punctured. The real world is not a Monte Carlo simulation in an ivory tower; the destructive power of black swans far exceeds the expectations of mathematical equations. Final Question: Was it all really worth it? Decision-making distortions and winner narratives in crisis. Eli Goldfine: We only have a few minutes left. I want to ask a very soul-searching question: Considering the shocking collapse of FTX, but at the same time, the FTX Future Fund funded a massive number of cutting-edge technology and security projects, including Anthropic, in its early stages. Looking back at the whole ordeal, was it really worth it on a macro level? Sam Bankman-Fried: No. I'd love to give a self-deceptive yes, but I can't honestly say it was. I think it should have been. If I hadn't messed things up at the last minute, if those risk defenses hadn't crumbled, it could have been a huge force driving the world forward. Perhaps it retains some cautionary value if future generations can learn the right lessons from this disaster, but in reality, most people aren't learning anything. Eli Goldfine: What are the real lessons people should learn? Sam Bankman-Fried: The core lesson is just one: how distorted the decisions people make in extreme panic when a crisis truly arrives and the situation is completely out of control. Under the pressure of life and death, people lose their judgment about what truly matters at an alarming rate, and all rules crumble in an instant. And after the dust settles, history is always written by the victors. The causal details of every event are reshaped, distorted, and simplified through the victor's lens. For those outside the storm, it's virtually impossible to penetrate the fog of the victor's narrative to uncover the true mechanisms. A survival guideline for the new generation of 14-year-olds: Stop doing quantitative trading on Wall Street, dedicate yourself to AI. Eli Goldfine: As a 14-year-old facing the coming era of superintelligence, what is your core advice for me if I want to create the greatest positive value in this world? Sam Bankman-Fried: Ten years ago, the standard answer from the effective altruistic community would have been "Earning to Give": go to Wall Street, do high-frequency trading, make billions of dollars, and then donate the wealth to charity. But times have completely changed. At this juncture approaching the singularity, high-frequency trading on Wall Street is no longer the most important battleground. The window between now and the full-fledged takeoff of AI is narrowing rapidly, and the value of deeply understanding and harnessing machine intelligence is rising exponentially. Whether it's dedicating yourself to cutting-edge AI alignment and security research, or finding a piece of traditional infrastructure and fully automating it with AI, delving into the core of machine intelligence is the only truly worthwhile battleground in this era.

data.title: Four checks a week: The printing press slows down as Tether begins investing.
data.description:
Author: Daisy, Deep Tide TechFlow

From November 16th to 19th, Tether signed four checks in four days.

The first was in Brazil, where Tether Capital led the Series C round for USD account service provider Nomad, investing $15 million, bringing the total round to 172 million reais and valuing the company at 4 billion reais post-money.

The second was for Stables, a payment infrastructure company that processes over $2 billion in USDT transactions annually, focusing on Asia and the Middle East and North Africa.

The third was in Singapore, where Tether and Abu Dhabi's Further Asset Management jointly invested approximately $10 million in MetaComp.

The fourth transaction was in Switzerland, targeting SCRYPT, one of the largest stablecoin trading and liquidity providers in the country. All four companies are doing the same thing: facilitating the flow of US dollars across borders. Two weeks before signing these checks, Tether had just released its third-quarter report. The printing press has slowed down. As of September 30, Tether had $191.5 billion in reserve assets, including $132.4 billion in US Treasury bonds, and a net operating profit of $4.5 billion for the first nine months of this year. While these figures still seem large, Tether's net profit for the first three quarters of the same period last year had already exceeded $10 billion. The statistical methods used in the two years are different; last year, net profit was reported, while this year, net operating profit is reported, so they cannot be directly subtracted. The profits for the first three quarters of this year were $1.04 billion, $1.5 billion, and $1.5 billion, respectively. At this rate, it will be difficult to return to the high point of over $13 billion in 2024 for the whole year. More importantly, another figure is that the issuance of USDT in the first three quarters of this year has basically stopped at $184 billion. Tether's business can be broken down into a multiplication, that is, the circulating scale of USDT multiplied by the yield on US Treasury bonds. For every $1 deposited by a user, Tether uses it to buy short-term US Treasury bonds to earn interest. The Federal Reserve began cutting interest rates in the fall of 2024, and the yield variable has been declining; this year, the scale variable has also remained unchanged. With both variables stuck, profits can only fall. Tether can't control interest rates; all it can do is push the scale back up. Relying on the existing cryptocurrency holdings on exchanges to support the next $100 billion is unrealistic. New scale can only come from real wages, payments, remittances, and daily bills outside the cryptocurrency sphere. To absorb this money, there needs to be a channel. Instead of teaching users, it directly invests in the channels. Tether realized early on that it's virtually impossible to teach everyone in the world how to download wallets, write mnemonic phrases, and calculate on-chain transaction fees. So it simply stopped teaching and directly invested in the financial apps that users were already using. This strategy began to take shape in 2024. In April of that year, Tether restructured into four major sectors: Data, Finance, Power, and Edu, and its investments began to have clear industry objectives. In June of the same year, it invested $18.75 million in Taipei-based XREX, specifically for compliant USDT cross-border B2B payments, serving SMEs in emerging markets. Subsequently, the checkbook expanded along the map of high inflation, foreign exchange controls, and remittance demand. In Africa, in October 2025, Tether invested in Kenya's Kotani Pay, a company that integrates blockchain applications with mobile wallets and local banking systems across Africa. In Latin America, in April, it led a $14 million Series A funding round for the Argentine crypto-finance platform Belo; in July, it invested $20 million in Mercado Bitcoin, a Brazilian on-chain financial platform serving 4.5 million users, and also disclosed a $20 million stake in the funding round for the Argentine digital bank Ualá. The Ualá investment best illustrates Tether's intentions. This bank has over 11 million customers, but due to local regulatory restrictions, USDT will not be integrated in the short term. Tether is still investing. Even if integration is not possible immediately, it will still acquire shares, and when regulations ease, it will already be on the shareholder list. The same applies to Nomad, which was signed this week. Nomad has 3.8 million customers and manages approximately 8 billion reais in assets. The integration of USDT and the gold token XAUT is still in the exploratory stage, and no launch date has been announced. However, these customers were already holding US dollars, so Tether saved several years' worth of customer acquisition costs. Brazil is also one of the most active markets for stablecoins, with stablecoins accounting for approximately 80% of the declared cryptocurrency trading volume in Brazil in 2025. Users still open the familiar local app; the interface and brand haven't changed, only a US dollar settlement channel has quietly been added in the background. If you can't get a license, invest in those who do. The longer the pipeline, the more difficult it is to circumvent regulation. On June 30, 2024, the EU's MiCA stablecoin terms came into effect, and on December 30, MiCA was fully implemented. USDT did not obtain EU authorization, and licensed exchanges in Europe successively restricted or delisted its trading. Tether chose to circumvent this. In November, it stopped issuing the euro-denominated stablecoin EURT, instead supporting third-party projects in Europe and promoting its own tokenization platform, Hadron. In November 2024, it announced an investment in Quantoz, a Dutch central bank-licensed electronic money institution; in December, it invested in StablR, which issues compliant stablecoins EURR and USDR, both using Hadron. USDT couldn't enter Europe, but Tether's technology and capital did. In February of this year, it made a strategic investment of $100 million in Anchorage Digital, a US federally licensed crypto bank. Anchorage is the issuer of the US-compliant stablecoin USA₮, which launched on January 27th. USDT remains overseas, while USA₮ is issued by a licensed bank—two parallel lines. While the European and American markets require indirect investment, in Switzerland and Singapore, with their relatively open regulatory frameworks, Tether directly invests in licensed institutions. This week's signing of SCRYPT, which has been operating under the supervision of the Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority (FINMA) and the self-regulatory organization VQF since 2019, and MetaComp, which holds a major payment institution license from the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), will directly expand its compliance and cross-border channels. Rather than applying for licenses from scratch, Tether prefers to directly invest in institutions that already hold licenses. Tether is even looking towards non-human users. On October 15th, Tether Capital made a strategic investment in AIsa. On this platform, companies can set spending limits for AI agents, allowing them to purchase data, software, and computing power independently. Currently, the platform has over 250,000 agents and has processed over 100 million transactions. This type of small-amount, high-frequency, 24/7 machine settlement is difficult to process through traditional bank accounts, making stablecoins the most direct payment tool. A Payment Company That Doesn't Rely on Transaction Fees for Survival: Looking at Tether's investments from 2024 to 2026 reveals a fundamental difference in cost structure between Tether and traditional payment companies. Tether holds only minority stakes in most of its investment companies; Adecoagro, a Latin American agricultural company in which it holds approximately 74.8%, is a rare exception and has little to do with payments. Stripe, PayPal, and remittance companies around the world rely on transaction fees charged to merchants to cover operating costs and bad debts; transaction fees are their lifeblood. Tether's recurring profits come from US Treasury bonds and repurchase agreement interest. It doesn't need to take a cut from every payment; as long as USDT is actually used, its reserve size will increase accordingly. Therefore, it can exchange equity for channels or lower the barrier for partners to use USDT by paying money. In February 2025, Tether led a $3 million pre-seed round for MANSA. MANSA specifically uses USDT to provide pre-financing liquidity to payment companies, allowing them to complete cross-border settlements instantly without having to deposit large sums of money in various locations. Traditional channel providers have also seen this gap; Stripe has acquired the stablecoin infrastructure company Bridge to enter the market itself. However, Stripe is essentially a payment company that collects transaction fees, while Tether does not expect to make money from the payment process, so it is naturally more willing to offer lower fees. The switch is in someone else's hands. This approach also has its limitations. USDT has been delisted in Europe, and Ualá has yet to integrate it. In the US market, it can only be issued via USA₮. Tether can pay to become a shareholder, but it can't turn on the regulatory switch for different countries. The further the pipeline extends into licensed banks and payment institutions, the more it encounters the most sensitive capital controls, anti-money laundering regulations of sovereign states, and a dollar clearing network that bypasses the traditional bank correspondent banking system. Currently, central banks still regulate stablecoins as crypto assets. Once USDT truly flows into wages and loans, the regulatory standards will shift to systemically important financial infrastructure. The interest printing press is still running, but at a significantly slower pace. Every check Tether signs around the world has a clear purpose: to channel more real dollars into its pipeline. How much of this pipeline will ultimately function is not in Tether's hands.
